title: Structural and biochemical characterization of Grimontia hollisae thermostable direct hemolysin with DNA reveals first Vibrio hemolysin with nuclease activity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded the Europe PMC supplement zip (18.3 MB) and listed it: one 18.0 MB PDF plus 14 figure images, no tables in any machine-readable format (no CSV/TSV/XLSX at all). Queried the Protein Data Bank (PDB, the public archive of experimental 3D structures) entry 9LCS via its REST interface and confirmed the coordinate file 9LCS.cif downloads (HTTP 200, chemical/x-cif); the other five accessions are listed in the paper's data availability statement.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All quantitative measurements: the relative nuclease activities of 12 point mutants (W65A, Y87A, K88A, D89A, Y107A, Y87A/Y107A, K88R, K88H, K88E, K88D, K88Q, K88N), shown as bar graphs in Figure 4H; the ~8 dissociation constants (14.8 and 22.4 micromolar for wild type and K88A on stem-loop double-stranded DNA, 2.39-5.01 micromolar on single-stranded polymers) read from the Results text; the ~16 DNA/RNA substrate sequences in Supplementary Table S1 and crystallography statistics in Supplementary Table S3, which exist only inside the 18 MB PDF.

a1_downloadable.note: The six crystal structures download freely from the PDB (I pulled 9LCS). But the data availability statement says 'All other data are available from the corresponding author on request', and the assay numbers are only inside a figure-and-text PDF, so the measurement data itself is effectively request-only.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no table of labels anywhere. The only candidate outcome - relative nuclease activity per mutant - is drawn as bars in Figure 4H and would have to be reconstructed by reading numbers off an image; the binding constants are sentences in the Results. The label would have to be built, which is the A2 failure condition.

a3_inputs_present.note: Protein sequence is available (GenBank WP_040528653.1) and the structures carry coordinates and bound single-stranded DNA; DNA substrate sequences are written out in Supplementary Table S1 inside the PDF.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated in the text where numbers appear: micromolar for dissociation constants, percent of wild-type for relative activity, angstroms for resolution.

a5_enough_rows.note: Six crystal structures, 12 single/double point mutants with an activity value, about 16 DNA substrates and roughly 8 binding constants. Tens of measurements in total against a threshold of about 1,500 labelled rows (400 for classification).

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~30 MB (six mmCIF coordinate files plus an 18 MB PDF)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small; laptop size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Six PDB accessions text-mined by Europe PMC match the six listed in the data availability statement, and 9LCS resolves to this paper's citation in the PDB record.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels that do exist are real physical measurements - gel-based exonuclease assays and bio-layer interferometry binding kinetics - not another model's output. Provenance is fine; there is simply almost none of it.

existing_models.name: CLAPE-DB (contrastive learning on a pretrained protein language model, predicts which residues of a protein touch DNA)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported area under the receiver-operating curve of 0.871 and 0.881 on two standard protein-DNA binding benchmarks (PDNA-type sets); split quality not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved beyond the abstract; generalisation to proteins with no homologue in training is the usual stated gap.

existing_models.name: GPSite (one network predicting binding residues for DNA, RNA, peptides, metals and more from sequence-derived structure)
existing_models.score_and_split: Published as a genome-scale binding-site annotator in eLife; numbers not read by me, only the abstract-level description.

existing_models.name: TransBind (alignment-free language-model predictor of DNA-binding proteins and residues)
existing_models.score_and_split: Communications Biology 2025; claims precise detection from a single sequence without multiple-sequence alignments. Numbers not read by me.

existing_models.name: Pore-forming-toxin support vector machine classifier (reduced-alphabet sequence features)
existing_models.score_and_split: About 81% accuracy on its own pore-forming-toxin versus non-toxin set, split details not checked.

existing_models.name: MultiToxPred 1.0 / ToxDL 2.0 (protein toxin class predictors)
existing_models.score_and_split: MultiToxPred classifies 27 toxin mode-of-action classes with a gradient-boosting ensemble; ToxDL 2.0 uses a protein language model plus graph neural network. Scores not read by me.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model, small CPU-runnable checkpoints)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be ample, but there are only tens of labelled examples, so a frozen-embedding head would have nothing to fit.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; irrelevant here because the dataset is too small.

integration.partner_dataset: UniProt plus the Protein Data Bank protein-DNA complex sets used by CLAPE-DB and GPSite
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do pore-forming toxin folds carry cryptic nuclease active sites that residue-level DNA-binding predictors systematically miss - a question these six structures could seed but not answer, since they supply six positives and no negatives.

controls.positive_control: The paper itself supplies one: Lys88 must come out as the most important residue, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus TDH must be flagged as nuclease-positive. But a single conserved residue in one protein is an anecdote, not a control set.
controls.negative_control: None available - no TDH-family members were tested and found to lack nuclease activity, so there are no measured negatives.
controls.external_validation: None in this paper beyond the one V. parahaemolyticus homologue; an external set would have to be assembled from other papers.

honest_claim_h3: Nothing beyond 'in this single toxin, Lys88 is required for DNA cleavage' could be claimed from these data; any model trained on them would be describing twelve mutants of one protein.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use protein sequence and structure to predict which bacterial pore-forming toxins also cut DNA.
plain_idea.train_on: What was considered: the toxin's protein sequence (and its predicted or crystal structure) for each member of the thermostable direct hemolysin family across Vibrio and relatives. Verified count of labelled examples here: 6 structures of one protein and 12 point mutants with an activity number locked in a figure.
plain_idea.predict: Whether the protein has 3-prime-to-5-prime exonuclease activity (chews DNA from one end), and how strongly. The truth would come from gel-based cleavage assays and bio-layer interferometry binding measurements like the ones in this paper - each one a bench experiment on purified protein.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Structural biologists and bacterial-pathogenesis labs would learn whether a toxin fold hides a second enzymatic function, which would redirect which homologues they purify next. As posed here it fails on data volume, not on interest.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper adds six structures of one protein; the existing residue-level DNA-binding predictors were trained on hundreds of protein-DNA complexes (one cited benchmark has 646 training proteins, about 15,600 binding sites).

confidence_score.why: Replicate counts for the gel assays are not in any machine-readable file, and with about 12 mutants there is no way to calibrate per-prediction uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: CLAPE-DB, GPSite and TransBind are 2024-2025 language-model-based systems with reported areas under the curve near 0.88 on shared benchmarks; nothing in these six structures provides leverage against them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition in spirit and the second outright: this paper contributes six positive examples of one protein and no negatives, so a model seeing them plus the existing training data gains essentially nothing measurable.

ml_idea: The only coherent task would be predicting cryptic nuclease activity in pore-forming toxin folds from sequence or structure, with this paper supplying the seed positives. That needs a labelled family-wide assay panel that does not exist; the paper itself provides six structures and about twenty hand-read numbers.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: six mmCIF files and one PDF total about 30 MB; eight hours is the cost of digitising bar-chart activity values and transcribing PDF tables by hand, which is itself the reason to reject.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the labelled rows that exist in machine-readable form. Answer: zero - the supplement is a single 18 MB PDF of figures, and the only deposited data are six crystal structures.

verdict_reason: A classic single-protein structural biology paper: six crystal structures, about twelve mutant activity values that live inside a figure, and no tabular data at all. Fails A5 (tens of measurements against a 1,500-row bar) and A2 (the label would have to be digitised off bar graphs), with the data availability statement also routing everything else through the corresponding author.
